candidato.titulo: CDK1 protein offers clues to which breast cancers will resist targeted therapy
candidato.resumo: Researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research have discovered that the activity of a protein called CDK1 in breast cancers is linked to how they respond to a common therapy—an insight that could inform more personalized treatment approaches for patients.

texto_fonte:
CDK1 protein offers clues to which breast cancers will resist targeted therapy
Researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research have discovered that the activity of a protein called CDK1 in breast cancers is linked to how they respond to a common therapy—an insight that could inform more personalized treatment approaches for patients.
The study, published in Advanced Science, looked at estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer—the most common type, fueled by the hormone estrogen. Many people with this cancer now receive drugs called CDK4/6 inhibitors alongside hormone therapy. These drugs stop cancer cells from multiplying, but they don't work for everyone, and in advanced cancer, eventually stop working for most patients.
"CDK4/6 inhibitors have made a real difference for people with breast cancer, but right now we can't tell who will get the most out of them, or whether they've stopped working," says Associate Professor Liz Caldon, lab head at Garvan and co-senior author of the study. "We wanted to find a signal in the tumor itself that tells us who is most likely to benefit and whether the therapy is doing its job."
Is the engine on?
CDK1 belongs to the same family of proteins as CDK4 and CDK6, which control when cells divide. CDK4 and CDK6 set the process in motion, while CDK1 is needed for the final stage, when the cell splits in two. Healthy cells divide this way—cancer is what happens when that process runs out of control.
Caldon explains, "CDK1 is like the 'engine' that has to start for a cell to divide. CDK4/6 inhibitors work by jamming the cell's ignition, but some cancer cells find a way to 'hotwire' around it. Even then, the cell can only divide if the CDK1 engine is running—so checking whether it's switched on shows whether the drugs are still holding the cancer back."
To follow CDK1 as breast tumors grow, the team developed a new preclinical model carrying a fluorescent sensor that lights up whenever the protein is active. Using it, they found CDK1 activity rose as tumors became invasive.
"Most tests can tell you whether a protein is there, but not whether it's actually working," says Dr. Max Nobis, co-senior author of the study, now a lab head and lecturer at the University of Manchester. "This model shows us which cells have CDK1 switched on, so we can track the cell cycle being activated during treatment."
In more than 400 patients' breast cancer biopsy samples, the researchers also found CDK1 activity rose as the cancer became more aggressive, and higher activity was linked to worse outcomes.
Spotting cancers that become resistant
The researchers then used existing clinical trial data to investigate breast cancers that had been treated with CDK4/6 inhibitors. In tumors that didn't respond, the genes for CDK1 and its partner proteins stayed switched on—an indirect sign the CDK1 engine was still running. The same activity appeared in advanced cancers that grew back despite treatment.
Breast cancer cells grown in the lab with a CDK4/6 inhibitor for around 10 months, until they became resistant, had also restarted their CDK1 engine, and in the preclinical model, tumors that kept growing despite treatment showed higher CDK1 activity.
"It can take only a small number of surviving cells to bring a cancer back, so being able to see which ones are still active gives us a new view of how treatment resistance starts," says Professor Paul Timpson, co-senior author and co-director of Garvan's Cancer Ecosystems Program.
"CDK1 kept turning up as a red flag—in early breast cancer, in advanced cancer and in cancers that had overcome treatment," says Dr. Sarah Alexandrou, first author of the study. "If a tumor has high CDK1, that may be a sign CDK4/6 inhibitors won't work as well, which is something doctors could one day use when planning each patient's care."
Building on decades of research
The work follows Garvan research in the 1990s showing how a related protein, cyclin D1, drives breast cancer growth—findings that helped make the case for CDK4/6 inhibitors years before they reached patients.
"Finding better options for people whose cancer stops responding to treatment takes long-term commitment," says Caldon. "Over many years, our lab has built a collection of breast cancer cells that have become resistant to different drugs, and each one takes many months of careful work.
"These models are where we saw CDK1 switching back on, and our hope is that tracking CDK1 will help doctors match each person with the treatment most likely to work for them."
The team says the findings now need to be tested in larger groups of patients treated with CDK4/6 inhibitors, and could eventually open the door to new drugs targeting CDK1.
"Decades ago, CDK4/6 inhibitors were just an idea—now they're helping people with breast cancer around the world," says Timpson. "There's no drug for CDK1 yet, but that doesn't mean there won't be one day."
Publication details
Sarah Alexandrou et al., Tracking CDK1 Dynamics With a Novel Biosensor Mouse and Clinical Cohorts to Predict CDK4/6 Inhibitor Sensitivity in ER+ Breast Cancer, Advanced Science (2026). DOI: 10.1002/advs.77920
Journal information: Advanced Science

candidato.titulo: A protein that regulates mRNA decoding can itself be regulated with implications for understanding cancer
candidato.resumo: Decoding of messenger RNA (mRNA) occurs during translation, the vital cellular process that builds proteins. Errors in this process are known to lead to cancer growth. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital identified how one factor involved in mRNA decoding can be altered, identifying potential cancer origins and new targets for KRAS-related treatment resistance. The results are published in Nature Cell Biology.

texto_fonte:
A protein that regulates mRNA decoding can itself be regulated with implications for understanding cancer
Decoding of messenger RNA (mRNA) occurs during translation, the vital cellular process that builds proteins. Errors in this process are known to lead to cancer growth. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital identified how one factor involved in mRNA decoding can be altered, identifying potential cancer origins and new targets for KRAS-related treatment resistance. The results are published in Nature Cell Biology.
To add the correct building block to a protein, the ribosome (the molecular machine that makes proteins) reads codons (a grouping of three nucleotides) in a process called mRNA decoding during translation elongation. The translation elongation factor eEF1A influences the speed and accuracy of mRNA decoding. It was known that, in certain tumors, the METTL13 enzyme modifies eEF1A at lysine 55 (eEF1AK55me2), thus increasing protein synthesis and promoting tumor growth. How eEF1AK55me2 affects translation elongation and contributes to tumor growth was unknown.
"We worked collaboratively with our co-authors to create cell lines that lacked METTL13 to recombinantly express eEF1 with and without METTL13-mediated methylation," said co-corresponding author Scott Blanchard, Ph.D., St. Jude Department of Structural Biology. "We then leveraged the power of parallelized single-molecule imaging experiments to demonstrate that eEF1AK55me2 affects mRNA decoding in a way that rationalized our collaborators' observations in quantitative, kinetic and structural terms."
Solving the eEF1AK55me2-METTL13 axis
The work built upon findings from a study the St. Jude team published in Nature in 2023, in which they used cryo-electron microscopy to determine the atomic structure of human ribosomes bound to eEF1A and compared mRNA decoding in human and bacterial translation. That study created a foundation to examine the effect of the eEF1AK55me2-METTL13 axis on translation.
Through proteomic profiling and single-molecule imaging, the team found that the axis promotes efficient translation of a subset of codons that are enriched in oncogenes, such as KRAS. Because KRAS is an oncogenic driver present in many tumor types, understanding how it is expressed and how it develops resistance to standard-of-care treatments is of interest to the oncology field. The team further examined METTL13 disruption as a potential target to overcome KRAS-related treatment resistance and observed stymied growth of KRAS-inhibitor–resistant tumors in animal models.
These findings have implications for developing future treatment strategies in which METTL13 could be used as a target to inhibit KRAS production in tumors. In healthy preclinical models, it was found that knocking out METTL13 does not cause toxic effects, a significant positive feature for potential clinical use.
"Our team's research demonstrates that this methyltransferase stimulates the translation of KRAS and other proliferation-promoting proteins. Reducing production of KRAS, a known driver of many cancers, can be achieved by knocking down METTL13 using a drug or some other mechanism, so that KRAS-driven cancer patients can have a better chance of survival," said Blanchard.
Varying elongation rates have critical impact
The team also discovered that the speed of elongation varies, with critical impacts on protein production.
"There is a growing understanding that protein synthesis occurs at rates that are not uniform. In our findings, we showed that even two related codons, encoding the same amino acid but differing in the third nucleotide position, can show different decoding speeds in a manner that depends on eEF1A K55 methylation," said Blanchard. "When METTL13 is present and eEF1A K55 is methylated, the two related codons are decoded at very similar rates; when METTL13 is absent, the codons are decoded at different rates."
The presence of METTL13 as a possible prognostic tool
To examine how the presence of METTL13 influenced other aspects of cancer development, the team examined its effect on patient prognosis. They compared preclinical models in which METTL13 disruption prevented tumor growth with outcome data from patients with lung adenocarcinoma and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, tumors in which METTL13 is often amplified. They observed that increased methyltransferase activity correlated with poor prognosis.
"We found that you can look for the activity of this methyltransferase in cancer, because high activity of METTL13 seems to correlate with aggressive cancer and lower survival," said co-first author Aaron Cruz-Navarrete, Ph.D., St. Jude Department of Structural Biology. "Our results show there's a potential to use the activity of this methyltransferase as a prognostic tool."
Publication details
Shuo Liu et al., Methylated eEF1A selectively decodes mRNA to shape cancer proteomes, Nature Cell Biology (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41556-026-02085-6

candidato.titulo: Armored caterpillars offer robot designers lessons in crossing slippery glass
candidato.resumo: Animals have long been one of the primary sources of inspiration for robotics researchers. This is because they rely on sophisticated biological mechanisms and locomotion strategies that could be artificially reproduced in robots to equip them with desired capabilities.

texto_fonte:
Armored caterpillars offer robot designers lessons in crossing slippery glass
Ingrid Fadelli
Author
Animals have long been one of the primary sources of inspiration for robotics researchers. This is because they rely on sophisticated biological mechanisms and locomotion strategies that could be artificially reproduced in robots to equip them with desired capabilities.
Caterpillars, the wormlike larvae that later develop into butterflies or moths, have also attracted the attention of many roboticists. Their elastic bodies and their ability to stick onto many types of surfaces allow them to move in complex natural environments and squeeze through narrow openings.
Caterpillars adapt their movements based on what they are crawling on, as they might not always adhere perfectly to each surface. Researchers at the University of Naples Federico II and the University of Palermo recently assessed how well caterpillars moved on wood, steel, slate and glass, observing how they coped with more challenging conditions.
The team improved a mathematical model introduced in one of their previous papers, which represents the body of caterpillars as masses connected by springs. Guided by the model, they then fitted real caterpillars with artificial armor to increase their body stiffness and added weights to improve friction and adhesion.
The results of the team's experiments led to the identification of strategies that could allow robots to attach themselves and move on various materials. Their paper, published in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface, may guide the development of new nature-inspired soft crawling robots.
"Building on previous studies, this work employs a crawling model that represents the body as spring-linked masses, interacting with the environment via threshold-based adhesion and Winkler-like springs," wrote Mario Argenziano and his colleagues in their paper.
Observing caterpillars crawling on distinct surfaces
Argenziano and his colleagues built on their previously introduced model of caterpillar crawling. They tested the model's predictions experimentally by observing caterpillars from the species Pieris brassicae as they crawled on wood, steel, slate and glass.
"Our results highlight a strong correlation between substrate roughness and crawling performance," wrote the authors. "While caterpillars seamlessly adapt their movement to predominant surface patterns, they struggle on smooth surfaces like glass—where microscale asperities are insufficient for proleg grip—confirming that adequate adhesion is crucial to trigger and sustain movement."
Based on their initial observations and using their mathematical model, the researchers then developed artificial armor that would increase the stiffness of the caterpillars' bodies. They then fitted caterpillars with the armor, adding separate weights to increase friction and adhesion. They found that the armor and weights improved the insects' ability to crawl on smooth glass.
"Driven by the model's insights on these physical constraints, we explored how crawling mechanics could be artificially enhanced," wrote the authors. "Through proof-of-concept experiments, we equipped larvae with artificial armor to increase body stiffness and additional masses to improve effective friction and adhesion, allowing them to cross non-walkable glass surfaces."
Inspiring new crawling soft robots
The team's experiments yielded insights that could be useful for the development of caterpillar-inspired and other crawling robots. Most notably, they demonstrated that achieving a balance between body elasticity and the ability to adhere to surfaces is an essential aspect of effective crawling.
"These findings validate the model's predictive accuracy, envisioning possible novel design criteria for bioinspired soft crawlers capable of adapting movements in complex habitats," wrote the authors.
The mathematical model developed by Argenziano and his colleagues and the crawling principles they uncovered could prove useful for the development of soft robots that can effectively move on various surfaces and terrains. Future studies could try to reproduce the properties of the artificial armor created by the team in robotic systems.
Written for you by our author Ingrid Fadelli, edited by Gaby Clark, and fact-checked and reviewed by Robert Egan—this article is the result of careful human work. We rely on readers like you to keep independent science journalism alive. If this reporting matters to you, please consider a donation (especially monthly). You'll get an ad-free account as a thank-you.
Publication details
Mario Argenziano et al., Allowing caterpillar locomotion on any substrates: towards hybrid soft robots design, Journal of the Royal Society Interface (2026). DOI: 10.1098/rsif.2026.0288.

candidato.titulo: Remote code execution on Linux systems with multipath TCP
candidato.resumo: On October 27, LLM provider Anthropic reported on a remotely exploitable use-after-free bug affecting systems with multipath TCP listeners open. The bug works by triggering a response to a retransmitted SYN packet at the same moment that the TCP connection is established in another thread, causing the first thread to access the connection's options structure after the second thread has freed it. The first thread can then disclose kernel memory or cause a buffer overflow, writing an attacker-controlled payload. The fix was to only free the structure after an RCU grace period . On October 29, the Go security team advised that all programs written in Go use multipath TCP by default , so many systems may be unknowingly vulnerable. And, of course, there is always the possibility of related bugs in other sections of the TCP stack. Users may be wise to update to a patched kernel as soon as one becomes available for their distribution.

candidato.titulo: Benchmarking Nvidia’s Vera CPU for the data center — standalone Vera tested against Granite Rapids-AP and EPYC Turin
candidato.resumo: Nvidia gave us access to its Vera data center CPU for testing against Intel's Granite Rapids-AP and AMD's EPYC Turin.

texto_fonte:
Nvidia’s Vera CPU is an important next step in the company’s years-long spearheading of AI infrastructure buildout. It’s arriving just as the shift to agentic AI workflows has created unprecedented demand for data center CPUs, and it’s designed specifically for this moment, at least according to Nvidia’s marketing bullet points. Although the idea that anyone developed a CPU for a shift in demand that arose just six months ago is reaching, as our benchmarks below show, Nvidia’s claims about Vera aren’t full of hot air.
Based on the workloads we have now — there aren’t standardized end-to-end agentic benchmarks focused on the CPU right now — Vera has strong indicators about its usefulness in agentic workflows. It offers chart-topping performance in Python, for instance, which makes up much of the backbone of the AI software ecosystem.
It also shows commanding memory bandwidth, both at the socket level and system level, with the high-speed C2C interconnect between Vera chips. In contentious agentic environments where agents may be querying large databases, that bandwidth is critical.
Specialization is one thing, but Vera is arriving in a hotly contested server market with custom Arm chips penetrating the data center and the old guard of x86 chips from AMD and Intel, which not only have a foundation in the data center, but also an extensive list of clients that work with their systems. Regardless of how Vera performs, that’s no small undertaking.
What’s surprising about Vera isn’t that it performs well in these agentic-adjacent workloads, but that it offers competent performance in general-purpose server workloads as well, often managing to match or beat the comparable AMD Turin and Intel Granite Rapids-AP chips. The scales are more balanced when looking at frontend workloads, with the core density available on x86 CPUs often the winner, but Vera trades that density for strong performance in backend, data-rich operations.
It’s an impressive showing for Nvidia's first custom core, called Olympus, and a stark improvement in nearly all aspects over Grace, which used an off-the-shelf Arm core design. The 88-core CPU is built on the Armv9.2-A architecture, including two threads per core through Nvidia’s “spatial multithreading.”
The chip is characterized by a 10-wide decode, similar to Arm’s AGI, as well as Nvidia’s second-gen Scalable Coherency Fabric (SCF). You can read more about the SCF and the Olympus core in our Vera deep dive, but SCF is critical to Vera’s performance. It’s a mesh that distributes L3 across the die, offering up to 3.4 TB/s of bandwidth across the die.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Vera has high memory bandwidth as well, leveraging replaceable SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X at 9600 MT/s, offering up to 1.2 TB/s of total memory bandwidth or around 14 GB/s per core, more than double that of AMD’s dense Turin designs.
We’ve heard a lot about the speeds and feeds of Vera, however. It’s time to understand its role in the modern AI data center, as well as see how it performs in our benchmarks against the x86 competition before AMD’s Venice and Intel’s Diamond Rapids start rolling out.
Understanding the CPU's role in agentic AI
Depending on where you’re at in the fast-moving world of agentic AI, you probably have a different definition of what exactly an agentic CPU is. Given the rise in prominence of agentic CPUs, the understanding of what makes a CPU tick for this type of workload has been largely defined by two companies: AMD and Nvidia. Although the points they’ve driven about concurrency and the varied work of agents are correct, it’s useful to derive a definition from how we’re seeing agentic platforms deployed right now.
Let’s back up from there and look at real agentic workflows in action to better understand where CPUs fit into this chain. As we’ve seen with Meta Muse and OpenAI Dots, there’s a class of persistent agent that gives you a slice of compute in the cloud. These CPU-only racks communicate with inference servers to actually run the models, but their workload is defined by concurrency. It’s not about the performance of an individual sandbox but instead how each sandbox performs when the chip is fully loaded.
Concurrency provides important context to some of the workloads companies like Nvidia and AMD have described. Some tool calls are more demanding, like code compilation and large database queries, but reading/writing files, running code tests, and going online in a headless browser is not demanding CPU work in isolation. When the chip is handling potentially thousands of these tool calls, however, slight advantages start to pile up. And, the CPU topology plays a bigger role in how performance is sustained as agent sessions increase.
That’s one major tenet of an agentic CPU, one that can maintain performance with high concurrency. The other is variability, which touches on the CPU, but also the larger infrastructure available. Mark Lohmeyer, VP/GM of AI and computing infrastructure at Google Cloud, described an example to Tom’s Hardware about planning a vacation with an agent. Using AI to plan a vacation is just about as trite as examples get, but Lohmeyer sheds some light on the unique challenge of agentic workloads from the hyperscaler perspective.
In the example, Lohmeyer described planning a vacation over the course of a month, where he would suddenly prompt the agent to do a bunch of work, but may not return to prompt again for another week. “The actual use of the underlying compute, it's happening in basically bursts, right? There's like a burst of use at the start, maybe for an hour, and then it goes away, and then a couple days later, [it] bursts again for some other purpose and goes away,” Lohmeyer said. “They're very long-running workloads, effectively long-running, but often idle, basically.”
Agentic calls for a lot of power on demand, as the right alignment of this bursty work on a server with hardware contention can bring everyone’s sessions to a crawl. This factors into the type of work the CPU is doing, as well, which can include heavy code compilation, graph traversal, and large database queries. Scale that up across several agents, all with their own independent loops that don’t neatly align with each other, and the CPU problem for agentic AI becomes clear.
In the August 2026 study, Architectural Implications of Agentic AI Workflows, from researchers at The University of Texas at Austin and Microsoft Azure, the paper describes three tasks of the CPU in an agentic flow. In addition to a scheduler for GPU inference, which is how CPUs function in one-shot-style LLM queries, CPUs also serve as orchestrators for maintaining agent states and communication, and as runners that call tools and execute agent logic (often in Python).
The paper also shows this contention that can happen when multiple agents are running at once, passing requests to the GPU, receiving responses, acting, and then passing requests back. We’re looking at a cross-section of four agents over less than half a minute, and you can already see how small CPU-based tasks can align, as well as create hangs between GPU time.
Nvidia has been clear that Vera is an agentic CPU, though defining the performance of an agentic loop is still a work in progress. “The industry built a pretty good way to benchmark traditional workloads,” Lohmeyer said. “I think this is happening now for GPUs and TPUs for inference, for example. I think we're going to need the same type of industry-level benchmarks for agentic workloads that are probably still emerging.”
Standardized benchmarks that look at the full agentic loop aren’t available yet. We have our own internal tests that we’re running and hope to have data for soon, and we’ve seen some vendor-level benchmarking from companies like Modal, but the broader industry hasn’t come forth with a set of benchmarks for the end-to-end agentic loop along the lines of a SPEC or TPC yet.
Although those tests aren’t available yet, we can still look at CPU performance through the lens of an agentic workflow, prioritizing aspects of performance that are important for agentic loops. We can also look at common workflows for agents, including code compilation for coding agents and database performance for retrieval agents. We can look at things like JSON parsing through the simdjson library, evaluating how these CPUs parse the large JSON files agents use to communicate. And we can look at the foundation of much of the AI ecosystem with Python performance.
That’s the focus of our benchmarking here, to establish where Vera stands among the x86 competition from AMD and Intel in well-known benchmarks. Hopefully we’ll have the opportunity for further testing in the near future to evaluate full agentic loops once that testing procedure is finalized.
Although we’re evaluating performance through an agentic lens here, Nvidia did not limit what tests we could run nor place any stipulations on our coverage. We’re thankful to Nvidia for providing us with remote access to a dual-socket Vera system for the purposes of testing, but beyond configuration checks to ensure the platform was operating as expected, we were left to run the tests we wanted to run. That includes several tests that are applicable to agentic workflows, but also tests from our general server CPU benchmarking suite, including Java, cryptography, compression, and rendering performance.
A gentle reminder for readers
Servers are not client PCs. You have much smarter operators with deeper access to the hardware, and often a software stack that’s unique to the specific workload at minimum, and highly tweaked and optimized for that workload at a maximum. With client CPUs, we can say that an AMD X3D chip is the best for gaming, or that Intel’s latest flagship offers the highest single-threaded performance. Servers depend much more on use cases.
In a typical review, we’d say that X is better than Y for Z purpose, and back that up with data. Here, that commentary is more muted. The reality is that hyperscalers maintain large fleets with a variety of hardware that can fit any purpose, and enterprises need to choose the hardware best suited not only for their operations, but also for TCO and a list of at least a dozen other variables that are specific to that business.
Nvidia Vera SPEC CPU 2026 estimates
So far, the primary benchmark we’ve had for Vera is SPEC CPU 2026 intrate, so we ran the full SPEC CPU 2026 suite to check Nvidia’s performance claims, as well as look at floating point performance. For anyone who hasn’t read SPEC CPU benchmarks before, there are a few disclaimers before heading into the results.
All of the runs here are estimates, and that’s due to how SPEC reporting works. There are strict reporting rules, and we’re not reporting these results to SPEC directly. The charts say “estimated,” but the numbers aren’t a guess. We ran SPEC CPU 2026 following the standard testing procedure, using the same compiler and flags for each CPU.
For the compiler, we used GCC 15.2 with a few common flags, including link-time optimization and march/mcpu to expose the correct instruction support to the compiler. We also used the general-purpose jemalloc memory allocator across all of the tests we ran.
Starting with the overall intrate, this is a series of applications primarily dealing with integer operations instead of floats, and the SOP is to run a copy of the application on each thread available. The test looks at what a CPU is capable of with many applications running at once, measuring throughput.
Nvidia’s numbers aren’t dissimilar from our own. In the company’s white paper, it showed Vera ahead of the EPYC 9755 by 3%, and with our tests, Vera is ahead by 1.5%. Keep in mind the considerably higher 512-thread count of the 9755 system here against the 352-thread Vera system. Vera absolutely runs away with performance when breaking down the score per-core.
Despite the core density of Intel’s 512-thread Xeon 6980P in a two-socket configuration, it’s not in the conversation here. Retesting with oneAPI represented an impressive 10% increase in performance with Intel-optimized binaries, but even against optimized code, Vera is 8.6% ahead with generic GCC.
There are some tests where Vera steals the show in the above album, as well as some where it falls behind, reflective of the testing we have later in this article. You can see that GCC compiler performance and Python performance are particularly strong points, with Nvidia even beating out AMD’s top-of-stack EPYC 9965.
Elsewhere, there are some weaknesses. SEAL crypto provides a look at the weaker cryptography performance of Vera, which is reflected in our other testing. Zstd compression also shows Vera trailing AMD and Intel, which makes sense. In our separate Zstd testing, Vera offered impressive compression performance with Zstd but fell behind on decompression.
We were curious about float performance on Vera given that Nvidia led with the standard intrate suite in its initial benchmarks. Vera tops the charts here on the back of some particularly strong showings in some of the tests. Our estimated PALM numbers, for instance, show off Vera’s second-generation Scalable Coherency Fabric (SCF), while ROMS pushes on memory bandwidth. This strong memory performance shows up in Marian and LBM, as well. There are a couple of misses, notably FemFlow and CACTUS, but the overall performance picture is clear.
The throughput benchmarks are what matter here for chips in this class, but we also ran SPEC CPU 2026’s intspeed suite for some estimated results, scaling up to use every thread available. No one is realistically running a single application on servers utilizing every thread available like this, but the numbers are there to browse if you’re interested.
Nvidia Vera Python and AI benchmarks
If there’s any direct benchmark for agentic AI right now, it’s Python performance. There isn’t one universal language for AI agents, but Python (and, to a lesser extent, TypeScript) make up the foundational agentic frameworks like LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen. A strong agentic CPU right now is defined in part by strong Python performance, and Vera has exactly that.
Starting with a broad overview, you can see the total average test times for PyBench above, with Vera leading the pack. It’s 4% ahead of the EPYC 9755, which itself leads Intel’s Xeons and the larger 9965. Python is largely single-threaded, especially for these basic, built-in functions, so we see the 9755 pair leading the 9965 pair throughout all of our Python benchmarks.
PyPerformance provides a much more granular look at Python performance, evaluating start-up times for the Python interpreter, regular expressions, and even full Python applications. The story doesn’t change, however. Outside of a couple of misses in web server-focused tests, Vera tops the charts across the board.
The AI ecosystem right now is largely built on Python, so strong performance here is a good early indicator of strong AI performance in the data center. Of course, this space is rapidly evolving, and other languages are working their way into the ecosystem. For this moment, however, Python is critical, and it’s an aspect of performance Vera nails.
We also ran Llama.cpp with a CPU BLAS backend, checking text generation and prompt processing (at different token lengths) on the CPU using gpt-oss-20b-q8. For prompt processing, much of the process is handled on the GPU, so this pure-CPU benchmark isn’t totally representative of a real deployment. However, the CPU still plays a role here, particularly in tokenization.
Unsurprisingly, we can see the single 6980P topping the charts in prompt processing, with a 2P Xeon 6980P coming up in second place, likely on the back of Intel’s AI-specific ISA extensions. We expect AMD to further extend support for these instructions in Zen 6, which should level the playing field.
Nvidia Vera memory and compression benchmarks
Nvidia has touted the memory bandwidth of Vera as one of the chip’s strongest points, and the industry-standard STREAM memory bandwidth benchmark backs up those claims. Vera comes with a memory bus width more than twice as large as Grace, plus a large jump up to LPDDR5X-9600. It’s capable of up to 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth through the LPDDR5X interface, and up to 1.8 TB/s of bandwidth between Vera sockets.
AMD’s support for DDR5-6000 is relatively slow, and although Intel offers more bandwidth with MRDIMMs reaching up to 8,800 MT/s, Vera is in a league of its own here. That’s true without optimization, as well. After my initial STREAM pass, Nvidia suggested passing the OpenMP “spread” policy, which distributes processes as far away from each other as possible to reduce cache/memory contention.
With AMD and Intel, we see a slight regression with this setting, but it offers Vera a massive jump in memory bandwidth. Undoubtedly, the scales will start to level off as AMD and Intel roll out their next-gen Venice and Diamond Rapids parts, both of which tout much higher memory bandwidth than their predecessors.
Flipping over to the simple MBW bandwidth benchmark, we can see similarly strong performance from Vera, regardless of copy size.
The classic CacheBench benchmark flips the script, with Vera trailing the pack in the combined read / modify / write test. This weaker cache performance here is largely overshadowed by the memory bandwidth. The performance level is slightly below Nvidia’s contemporaries, but not by enough to make a significant difference.
Vera loses some points in compression workloads, which we see echoed in our SPEC runs in dedicated benchmarks. Using Zstd, Vera offers chart-topping compression performance at the default level 3 compression, as well as the maximum level 19 compression, across both standard and Long Mode runs. However, in decompression, the Turin chips take over, with Vera sitting alongside or below a dual 6980P configuration.
7-Zip traditionally favors Zen, so it’s no surprise to see both Turin configurations at the top of the charts. Vera loses out to the dual 6980P system in both compression and decompression performance via 7-Zip.
Nvidia Vera Java, database, and crypto benchmarks
Python is the language of choice for the AI ecosystem right now, but JavaScript/TypeScript are a close second. We ran three standard Java suites to evaluate performance: Java SciMark, DaCapo, and Renaissance.
Java SciMark is the best place to start. AMD wins out with the Zen 5-based 9755 in the composite score, but Vera maintains surprisingly strong positions in straight scientific operations, including FFTs, sparse matrix multiplies, and a Monte Carlo simulation. It falls behind in dense LU matrix factorization and Jacobi SOR.
DaCapo and Renaissance are both Java suites with a wide variety of real Java workloads, focused on native performance in DaCapo and VMs in Renaissance.
Database performance for Vera is strong across our ClickHouse and SQLite benchmarks. In max-thread SQLite, Vera is only beaten by a single-socket 6980P server, and it jumps into the lead in our like-for-like 64-thread and 128-thread tests. ClickHouse provides some interesting data that goes beyond a steady-state SQL database.
On the second and third runs of ClickHouse, Vera is competitive with a dual EPYC 9755 server, but from a cold cache, Vera is much faster, racking up an advantage of nearly 40% in the first run.
For bringing that data in, we measured JSON parsing speed with simdjson, which, as the name suggests, relies heavily on modern SIMD instructions. Turin has a natural lead here with its native AVX-512 execution.
In cryptography workloads, Vera falls behind the pack significantly in the John The Ripper password cracker, while trailing the massive core arrays of its competition in OpenSSL.
Nvidia Vera HPC and compilation benchmarks
HPC is usually the domain of dense CPUs, but Vera performs well in a variety of HPC tasks that we tested. In Discrete Fourier Transforms (DFT) using FFTE, Vera tops the charts, as it does in Octave and CloverLeaf. Although not strictly HPC, Vera falls in the middle of the pack in intensive mathematical operations like m-queens, and it trails chips with massive core arrays in the heavily threaded Primesieve.
Code compilation is a more contentious workload, with Vera trading blows against AMD and Intel depending on the workload. Starting with the compilers themselves, Vera takes a strong lead in a timed GCC compilation, beating out a dual 9755 system by 12%. It falls into last place in our LLVM compilation tests, however, both using standard Makefiles and Ninja. These tests measure the time it takes to compile the compiler itself, not the time it takes to compile an application with it.
Elsewhere, Vera shows up strongly in ImageMagick and PHP compiles while losing out slightly to the dual 9755s in Godot. Compiler performance is important to agentic AI given the prominence of coding agents, which often need to build software from source as part of an agentic coding workflow.
Nvidia Vera encoding and rendering benchmarks
Encoding and rendering workloads aren’t the focus of Vera, but we ran our standard list of benchmarks, which includes some rendering and encoding tests. Vera has strong performance here in some applications, though it certainly takes a backseat to the headline Python and memory performance shared earlier in this article.
The fight is between AMD and Nvidia here, with the 9755 and its full Zen 5 cores topping the charts in our AV1 encoding tests. With x265, Vera comes out on top, though by a margin lower than the 25%+ we can see the 9755s hold with AV1.
We normally run Blender, though there isn’t an official Arm Linux version available, so we skipped the test here. Instead, we have the cross-platform C-Ray and POV-Ray. Vera manages to outclass even the 768 threads available on a 2P EPYC 9965 server, both at 1080p and 4K. Vera also leads in POV-Ray, though on a technicality. Every server we tested was tightly coupled short of the 2P 6980P server.
For a more granular look, we have OSPRay, where Vera tops the charts in real-time path tracing, though falls short of the AMD and Intel flagships in real-time scientific visualization. The “dim_512” subset is worth drawing attention to. Strong AVX-512 performance allows AMD to offer three or even four times the performance of Vera in this workload.
Nvidia makes a delayed debut
Although Vera isn’t Nvidia’s first data center CPU, it’s the first one that the company is aggressively pursuing with the same fervor that it carries with its accelerators. It’s an impressive chip, often punching far above its weight class, especially in those workloads that can show off its unique capabilities and topology.
Still, it’s a single 88-core chip arriving in a market characterized by granular SKU lists to meet a wide range of specific workloads. Vera won’t be the right choice for all of them, which is something that Nvidia itself has already stated. “The world is not going to be served by one SKU of CPU. And that's not our intention,” said Nvidia’s Ian Buck when Vera was revealed in March.
That’s not the intention with Vera, but the performance against contemporary x86 CPUs shows that Nvidia’s new push into standalone data center CPUs has legs, more so than the various building-block-style Arm chips we’ve seen from hyperscalers, certainly. If nothing else, Vera demands some attention from AMD and Intel.
The x86 crew is responding shortly, with Zen 6 queued up to roll out through the end of the year and Intel’s Diamond Rapids targeting a 2027 release. As you can imagine, we'll be putting those chips through their paces as well.

MORE: AMD vs. Intel
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

candidato.titulo: Ghostly Cat’s Head Nebula lurks within sight of Hubble and Webb
candidato.resumo: The NASA/ESA Hubble and the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescopes recently stared at an eerie star-forming scene within the Carina Nebula, a massive gas and dust cloud located approximately 7500 light-years away from Earth. The two telescopes offer complementary views of the shadowy form, nicknamed the Cat’s Head Nebula, which reflects the 'magical'' process of star formation. Hubble’s visible-light view shows the cat as a dark, elongated dust pillar and hints of young forming stars, while Webb’s infrared-light imagery unveils many stars and other hidden details.

texto_fonte:
The NASA/ESA Hubble and the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescopes recently stared at an eerie star-forming scene within the Carina Nebula, a massive gas and dust cloud located approximately 7500 light-years away from Earth. The two telescopes offer complementary views of the shadowy form, nicknamed the Cat’s Head Nebula, which reflects the 'magical'' process of star formation. Hubble’s visible-light view shows the cat as a dark, elongated dust pillar and hints of young forming stars, while Webb’s infrared-light imagery unveils many stars and other hidden details.
Like a spectral form rising out of a cold mist, the Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have come across a hauntingly dynamic star-forming scene within the vast Carina Nebula, a diffuse star-forming region. The small, select area that was observed by both telescopes is nicknamed the Cat’s Head Nebula because of its resemblance to a cat sitting with its back toward the viewer. The 'head' of the cat is turned to the right, revealing a glowing eye.
The distinctive shape of the Cat’s Head Nebula has likely been sculpted over time by the intense ultraviolet radiation and winds from massive stars in the Carina Nebula. As this stellar feedback erodes the surrounding gas and dust, denser material within the feline-shaped pillar resists erosion, at least for now.
Hubble’s visible-light view shows the nebula as an opaque, dark brown pillar of dust. The cat’s glowing red eye may mark a young star that is still partially embedded in the dust. A ridge of hazy yellow seems to follow the edge of the filament’s right side. This bright rim is consistent with gas illuminated and ionised by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars, potentially driving photoevaporation. This wispy outline is a sign that energetic ultraviolet light from massive, hot stars is impinging on the gas, heating it up and essentially evaporating it.
The diffuse material surrounding the pillar glows blue and cyan above, shifting to yellow, orange, and red toward the bottom. Hubble’s filters capture light emitted by oxygen, hydrogen, and sulfur, along with starlight scattered by dust. These colour variations reveal a complex mix of excited gas, dust, and stellar illumination.
Piercing through dust’s darkness
Webb’s near- and mid-infrared images each offer different pieces of information to help create a more well-rounded understanding of the Cat’s Head Nebula. While the nebula’s overall structure is similar to the visible-light image, the filament becomes more transparent, and its complex surface structure becomes discernable in near-infrared light. On the cat’s left are ghostly wisps of dust and gas, delicate structures exposed to radiation from nearby massive stars.
The bright optical nebulosity visible to Hubble becomes less prominent in Webb’s near-infrared image. Instead, Webb’s near-infrared view reveals a dense scattering of stars that appear blue and yellow in this colour-composite image. Even in infrared light, some stars are still enshrouded in dust to various degrees. The cat’s eye remains conspicuous, while a faint jet-like feature near the cat’s belly could indicate an outflow associated with a young star.The cat’s eye is a more obvious example of an embedded star, while a faint jet protruding from the cat’s belly hints that a young star is located nearby, perhaps within the cat or externally just to its right.
In mid-infrared light, emission from warm dust and carbon-based molecules outlines intricate structures within the nebula. The filament’s bluish and greenish colours highlight emission that includes polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), carbon-based molecules excited by starlight. These variations in colour and brightness may reflect changes in PAH emission, dust continuum, and local irradiation, rather than temperature alone. Delicate globules and strands to the pillar’s left are particularly evident in this mid-infrared view.
To the right of the pillar, a bright light source appears yellow in the mid-infrared image. It lies against reddish emission from surrounding material. A narrow filament appears to cross the source, although the image alone cannot establish whether the two are physically related.
Though the Cat’s Head Nebula is a temporary scene that will eventually disperse, the region is packed with information. Hubble and Webb’s complementary views of the Cat’s Head Nebula are helping astronomers learn more about the elusive, chaotic, and complex process known as star formation.
More information
The Hubble Space Telescope is a project of international cooperation between ESA and NASA.
Webb is the largest, most powerful telescope ever launched into space. Under an international collaboration agreement, ESA provided the telescope’s launch service, using the Ariane 5 launch vehicle. Working with partners, ESA was responsible for the development and qualification of Ariane 5 adaptations for the Webb mission and for the procurement of the launch service by Arianespace. ESA also provided the workhorse spectrograph NIRSpec and 50% of the mid-infrared instrument MIRI, which was designed and built by a consortium of nationally funded European Institutes (The MIRI European Consortium) in partnership with JPL and the University of Arizona.
Webb is an international partnership between NASA, ESA and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA).

candidato.titulo: Quantum skyrmions outlast entanglement, hinting at more resilient networks
candidato.resumo: Quantum networks could one day connect quantum computers into more powerful systems and enable new forms of secure communication. But a fundamental obstacle stands in the way: Quantum information is extraordinarily fragile, and the entanglement between particles of light on which such networks would depend is easily disrupted.

texto_fonte:
Quantum skyrmions outlast entanglement, hinting at more resilient networks
Quantum networks could one day connect quantum computers into more powerful systems and enable new forms of secure communication. But a fundamental obstacle stands in the way: Quantum information is extraordinarily fragile, and the entanglement between particles of light on which such networks would depend is easily disrupted.
Now, in a new paper in Nature Physics, engineers at the University of Pennsylvania have demonstrated a potential workaround using topology, the branch of mathematics that famously considers a doughnut and a coffee mug equivalent because they both have a single hole that remains unchanged even when their shapes are distorted.
To explore whether topology's focus on properties that persist under deformation could lend resilience to quantum systems, the researchers built a chip that generates a pair of entangled photons, then gives one of them a distinctive pattern, known as a skyrmion, by polarizing its light in a particular way.
The researchers found that they could transfer the skyrmion's pattern engraved on a single photon locally to the quantum state shared by the two photons remotely. Even more surprisingly, when the researchers introduced enough disruption to sever the photons' entanglement, the topological property remained intact.
"It's as if one dancer's unique movement suddenly became part of a duet, and persisted even when the dancers were separated," says Liang Feng, professor in materials science and engineering (MSE) with a secondary appointment in electrical and systems engineering (ESE) and the paper's senior author. "If we can learn to encode information in such resilient patterns, that could lay the groundwork for much more reliable quantum networks."
The topology of quantum skyrmions
Unlike the hole in a doughnut, the defining topological feature of a quantum skyrmion isn't its physical shape, but a pattern in how its light is polarized.
"The light oscillates in different directions depending on where you inspect it," says Haoqi Zhao, a postdoctoral fellow at Yale, alumnus of Feng's lab and the paper's first author. "It's sort of like how regions of hair on your head grow in different directions."
In a quantum skyrmion, those variations form a pattern that encompasses all possible polarization states a fixed number of times. Even when individual parts of the pattern are disturbed, that number remains unchanged.
"Think of a swirl in someone's hair," says Zhao. "You can push individual strands out of place without changing the overall pattern."
Building a factory for quantum skyrmions
Prior work by other researchers has shown how to create these patterns involving individual photons, as well as skyrmions shared between entangled photons.
But no other team has demonstrated how to transfer a skyrmion's topological properties from a single photon to a quantum state shared by two photons, much less on the kind of small, scalable chip that could prove crucial to future quantum networks.
Nearly half a decade of refining techniques went into the chip's development, with the team fabricating prototypes in Penn's Singh Center for Nanotechnology.
"It's a bit like building an entire factory in miniature," says Yichi Zhang, a doctoral student in MSE and co-author of the paper. "One part of the chip generates entangled photons, another directs them where they need to go and still another creates the skyrmion pattern. The challenge was getting all the parts to work together."
Unexpected results
Once they had a working chip, the researchers deliberately introduced increasingly strong disturbances to the entangled photons they created, including unwanted background light.
As the interference increased, measurements showed that the quantum state deteriorated and the photons' entanglement eventually disappeared. But the skyrmion's defining topological property remained intact, only breaking down under still stronger disruption.
"Previous work suggested that these structures depended on entanglement," says Zhao. "Our findings show that the relationship is more complicated than we thought."
New possibilities, new questions
Beyond suggesting new ways to protect information in future quantum networks, the results also shed new light on the fundamental relationship between topology and quantum entanglement.
Even after entanglement disappeared, certain quantum correlations persisted, as indicated by a measure known as "quantum discord," suggesting a broader connection between more general forms of quantum correlations and topology.
"We've shown that these patterns can survive without entanglement, revealing a deeper role of quantum correlations beyond entanglement in quantum information processing," says Feng. "This discovery could not only deepen our understanding of quantum physics, but also help us develop new ways to protect quantum information."
Publication details
Haoqi Zhao et al., Chip-mediated manipulation of photonic quantum skyrmions, Nature Physics (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03487-x

candidato.titulo: Actor Patrick Stewart dies at 86, legendary star of Star Trek and X-Men
candidato.resumo: After his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, formally announced his passing, tributes poured in from around the world. Fans and former colleagues recalled his iconic roles and marveled at how easily he moved between commercial cinema and classical Shakespearean theater. Read Entire Article

texto_fonte:
RIP Patrick Stewart, the actor best known for playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the Star Trek franchise and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men movies, died Wednesday, October 28. He was 86. Stewart had Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, though neither diagnosis was made public until after his death.
After his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, formally announced his passing, tributes poured in from around the world. Fans and former colleagues recalled his iconic roles and marveled at how easily he moved between commercial cinema and classical Shakespearean theater.
Australian actor Hugh Jackman, who played Wolverine in the X-Men movies, called Stewart a "tremendous friend" and praised his contribution to the entertainment industry. "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days," he wrote on Instagram.
 – Hugh Jackman (@RealHughJackman) October 29, 2026
Another former co-star, English actor Ian McKellen, also mourned Stewart's death, describing him as a proud Yorkshireman and one of the most respected and beloved actors of his generation. In a long, heartfelt message on Instagram, McKellen said Stewart was "a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love."
Star Trek co-star William Shatner also remembered Stewart fondly, calling him "a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor." In a social media post, Shatner wrote, "What a heartbreaking week it has been," an apparent reference to the death of Walter Koenig earlier in the week. Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov in Star Trek, died October 25 at 90.
Praising Stewart's diverse body of work, Shatner said: "From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work... He will be deeply missed."
 – William Shatner (@WilliamShatner) October 29, 2026
Born in Mirfield, England, in 1940, Stewart's career got a boost when he joined the prestigious Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966. He appeared on the long-running British soap Coronation Street in 1967 and made his Broadway debut in 1971 in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Over the following decades, Stewart starred in a string of hit movies and TV shows, including Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol (1999), which earned him a Screen Actors Guild Award nomination for his portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge. He also played Captain Ahab in the miniseries Moby Dick (1998) and King Henry II in the film The Lion in Winter (2003), for which he received a Golden Globe nomination.
Stewart turned up on Frasier in the show's 11th and final season in 2003, playing a gay Seattle socialite and opera director who mistakes Kelsey Grammer's title character for a potential love interest. He also appeared on Top Gear and lent his voice to multiple characters on Fox's animated sitcom Family Guy.
His career drew awards from both critics and peers. He won three Laurence Olivier Awards between 1979 and 2008, as well as a Grammy in 1996 for Best Spoken Word Album for Children for his recording of Prokofiev's Peter and the Wolf. He was also nominated for a Tony Award, three Golden Globes, four Emmys and three Screen Actors Guild Awards.
Queen Elizabeth II knighted Stewart in 2010 for his services to drama. He was also an ambassador for the International Rescue Committee. His final on-screen performance will be a return as Professor Charles Xavier in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, due in theaters in December.

candidato.resumo: O Google anunciou nesta quinta-feira (29) uma nova ferramenta que permite criar, visualizar e editar documentos diretamente no Gemini, sem precisar sair da conversa com a inteligência artificial (IA). A novidade funciona no celular e na versão web do chatbot, com suporte a PDFs, apresentações, planilhas e outros formatos. Com a atualização, o usuário pode abrir uma prévia do arquivo dentro do próprio Gemini e fazer alterações manualmente ou solicitar modificações à IA. Também é possível selecionar trechos específicos para pedir ajustes no texto ou em elementos visuais. Segundo o Google, a ferramenta já está disponível para todos os usuários do Gemini, em todos os idiomas compatíveis com o aplicativo, incluindo o português. Entretanto, há diferenças entre os formatos aceitos no celular e no computador . Enquanto a versão para smartphones permite visualizar e editar arquivos PDF, o Gemini na web também oferece suporte a documentos do Google Docs, planilhas do Google Sheets, apresentações, arquivos Markdown, TXT e códigos de programação. Como funciona a edição de documentos no Gemini? A nova ferramenta permite trabalhar com arquivos diretamente na interface de conversa do Gemini. Depo

texto_fonte:
Sem sair do chat: Gemini ganha edição interativa de documentos no celular e na web
Por Marcelo Fischer |
O Google anunciou nesta quinta-feira (29) uma nova ferramenta que permite criar, visualizar e editar documentos diretamente no Gemini, sem precisar sair da conversa com a inteligência artificial (IA). A novidade funciona no celular e na versão web do chatbot, com suporte a PDFs, apresentações, planilhas e outros formatos.
Com a atualização, o usuário pode abrir uma prévia do arquivo dentro do próprio Gemini e fazer alterações manualmente ou solicitar modificações à IA. Também é possível selecionar trechos específicos para pedir ajustes no texto ou em elementos visuais.
Segundo o Google, a ferramenta já está disponível para todos os usuários do Gemini, em todos os idiomas compatíveis com o aplicativo, incluindo o português. Entretanto, há diferenças entre os formatos aceitos no celular e no computador.
Enquanto a versão para smartphones permite visualizar e editar arquivos PDF, o Gemini na web também oferece suporte a documentos do Google Docs, planilhas do Google Sheets, apresentações, arquivos Markdown, TXT e códigos de programação.
Como funciona a edição de documentos no Gemini?
A nova ferramenta permite trabalhar com arquivos diretamente na interface de conversa do Gemini. Depois de gerar um documento, o usuário pode expandir a prévia para a tela inteira e começar a fazer alterações.
É possível digitar diretamente no arquivo, selecionar partes do conteúdo e pedir que a inteligência artificial faça modificações específicas.
Por exemplo, o usuário pode solicitar que o Gemini crie um guia de estudos em PDF a partir de anotações feitas à mão e enviadas ao chatbot.
Depois que o documento estiver pronto, será possível revisar o conteúdo, destacar um trecho para pedir uma explicação mais detalhada ou solicitar mudanças na apresentação das informações.
A principal diferença em relação à experiência anterior é que o Gemini passa a oferecer uma interface interativa para revisar os arquivos gerados pela IA. Com isso, o usuário consegue acompanhar as alterações e continuar trabalhando no documento durante a conversa.
O recurso também permite combinar edições manuais com comandos em linguagem natural. Assim, quem estiver revisando um texto pode corrigir uma palavra diretamente no documento e, em seguida, pedir à IA que reformule outro parágrafo.
Conforme destacou o Android Authority, a versão web oferece a experiência mais completa neste primeiro momento, já que a edição no aplicativo para smartphones está restrita aos PDFs.
O Google não informou quando os demais formatos poderão ser editados pelo Gemini no celular.

candidato.titulo: Solid-state cooling advances toward practical use, but challenges remain
candidato.resumo: As temperatures rise, the need for cooling is growing worldwide. Conventional cooling systems consume large amounts of electricity and use refrigerants with a high global warming potential. Caloric cooling could offer a sustainable alternative by using solid-state materials instead of conventional refrigerants. Researchers at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), together with international partners, have analyzed the state of development of such systems.

texto_fonte:
Solid-state cooling advances toward practical use, but challenges remain
As temperatures rise, the need for cooling is growing worldwide. Conventional cooling systems consume large amounts of electricity and use refrigerants with a high global warming potential. Caloric cooling could offer a sustainable alternative by using solid-state materials instead of conventional refrigerants. Researchers at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), together with international partners, have analyzed the state of development of such systems.
Their review, published in Nature Energy, shows the progress achieved so far and the challenges that still stand in the way of practical deployment.
According to the German Meteorological Service, June 2026 ended with a historic heat wave. As such extreme events become more frequent worldwide, energy demand for space cooling is expected to more than double by 2050. The rapid development of artificial intelligence is also increasing cooling demand, as more powerful data centers generate more waste heat and must reliably protect their servers against overheating.
Cooling is becoming increasingly important not only in buildings and data centers but also in electronics, medicine and logistics. So far, this demand has mainly been met by vapor-compression systems. Although mature, this technology consumes large amounts of electricity and can cause noise through its compressors.
Research by Dr. Jingyuan Xu shows that there are other ways to cool. The early-career researcher heads the Zero-Emission and Environmentally Friendly Heating and Cooling Technologies research group at KIT's Institute of Microstructure Technology (IMT). Her expertise also informs the current review, which she led as the responsible author. "Caloric cooling offers two key advantages: It does not require refrigerants with a high global warming potential and can reduce energy consumption," Xu explains.
Progress in devices
Caloric cooling technologies use materials that heat up under external stimuli and cool down again when the stimulus is removed. Magnetic and electric fields can be used for this purpose, as can pressure or tensile strain. In a device, this change can be harnessed to absorb heat in one place and release it elsewhere, much like in a refrigerator.
Current prototypes show how far the field has developed. Some now achieve cooling powers that go beyond pure laboratory demonstrations: systems based on magnetic fields exceed three kilowatts, reaching a performance range relevant for larger cooling applications. Mechanically driven prototypes have passed the one-kilowatt mark. Smaller devices using electric fields could be suitable for electronics or wearables.
Despite major progress, a gap remains between the performance of the material and the cooling performance of the finished device: heat losses, material fatigue and incomplete work recovery during the cooling cycle reduce overall performance. "The material can show large temperature changes in the laboratory," says first author Dr. Kun Wang of IMT. "What matters, however, is how efficiently this effect can be used for cooling in a device."
Roadmap for practical deployment
In their study, the researchers show what caloric systems still need to provide reliable cooling in everyday use. Durability is particularly important. Devices have to remain stable over many millions of cycles if they are to cool reliably for years. It is also crucial that they can absorb and release heat quickly and require as little energy as possible for the cooling cycle.
In the short term, caloric systems will not replace established cooling systems across the board. "At first, they will be of interest where conventional cooling reaches practical limits," Xu explains. "This may be the case when devices need to operate very quietly or when refrigerants with a high global warming potential must be avoided." Standardized testing and application-oriented demonstrators will show which systems are suitable for these uses.
Publication details
Kun Wang et al., Caloric cooling devices and systems, Nature Energy (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41560-026-02143-1

texto_fonte:
Maior roubo da história: Binance perde US$ 6,3 bilhões em ataque hacker relâmpago
Por André Lourenti Magalhães • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
A corretora de criptomoedas Binance sofreu um ataque cibernético que resultou na perda de US$ 6,3 bilhões (ou R$ 34 bilhões, em conversão direta) em ativos financeiros na última quinta-feira (29). Especialistas atribuem a ação à Coreia do Norte e afirmam que este é o maior roubo da história do setor.
De acordo com a agência Reuters, toda a ação levou apenas 20 minutos. A investigação inicial apontou para uma vulnerabilidade no computador de um dos engenheiros que liberou acesso sem autorização para retirar o dinheiro, mas depois indicou que outros pontos de acesso foram comprometidos.
A Binance já atua em conjunto com autoridades nacionais e internacionais para investigar o caso e recuperar o prejuízo. Cerca de US$ 3 bilhões do valor perdido foram congelados, enquanto a empresa tenta retomar o montante restante.
Em comunicado oficial, a empresa afirma que usará os próprios fundos para cobrir as perdas.
O que acontece com quem tem ativos na Binance?
A empresa suspendeu os saques temporariamente por 48 horas como uma medida preventiva e garante que os ativos estão protegidos. Outros serviços da plataforma operam normalmente.
Em nota ao público brasileiro, a Binance diz que “os fundos de seus clientes permanecem seguros” e que segue requisitos de segregação do Banco Central do Brasil, nos quais criptomoedas são mantidas em cold wallets (carteiras frias, sem conexão com a internet) para ter uma camada de segurança extra.
